changes.old_en: ... to the presence of the name: the Essence in its unrestrictedness cannot be an object of knowledge. Even those names of the Essence which, in their aspect of non-otherness, are not distinguishable from It cannot be fully comprehended. The Prophet alludes to this with “or what You have reserved for Yourself in the knowledge of Your unseen.” Names of lordship, involving several mediations, cannot constitute the final reach of the perfected knowers.
changes.new_en: ... to the presence of the name: the Essence as unrestricted cannot be an object of knowledge. He further qualifies the name as one of the divine names, because the names of the Essence, insofar as they are not other than It, likewise cannot be objects of knowledge. The Prophet alludes to this with ‘or what You have reserved for Yourself in the knowledge of the unseen with You.’ The names of lordship cannot be the final goal of the perfected, owing to the many intermediaries involved.
changes.reason: Restores the omitted distinction between divine, essential and lordly names; لا يتعلق العلم بها is not merely failure of full comprehension.

changes.old_en: The relative pronoun qualifying “name” points to a limitation: even accomplished knowers do not encompass all divine names at once. Each has a special name as his Lord, and when he calls through that name he is answered. For him it is the Greatest Name. Hence reports of the Greatest Name differ between people. More comprehensively perfected persons receive numerous self-disclosures under many names, not being tied to only one.
changes.new_en: His expression ‘which’ stands in apposition to ‘name’. It indicates that the perfected cannot encompass all the names, since each is associated with a particular name that is his Lord: when he turns to it, he receives an answer. It is therefore the Greatest Name in his case. Accordingly, the Greatest Name varies according to persons, except for the perfected: they receive many self-disclosures from the names and are answered through many names, without being restricted to one name rather than another.
changes.reason: Removes invented distinction between ‘accomplished’ and ‘more comprehensively perfected’; preserves the received passage's apparent tension for the editorial note.

changes.old_en: Qūnawī corrects a possible misunderstanding: the knowledge and witnessing achieved under a particular divine name can be an endpoint relative to lesser grades, such as experiences mediated through the names of lordship; it is not the absolutely final endpoint. The unrestricted Essence itself has no terminus, nor any beginning. Beginnings and endings mark relative perfections: a beginning indicates a perfection appearing with respect to what follows, an end marks completion relative to what precedes. An unbounded Reality cannot be comprehended by a knower whose beginning and end are bounded.
changes.new_en: He then qualifies his statement to set the preceding issue right: the knowledge and witnessing arising from a tasting grounded in particular divine presences of the names are endpoints relative to the lower knowledge and witnessing arising from a tasting grounded in the names of lordship and what lies below them. They are not an absolute endpoint. The unrestricted Essence has no endpoint; how, then, could knowledge of It have one? Nor does It have a beginning: beginnings and endpoints attach neither to It nor to Its unrestricted perfection. Rather, they mark relative perfections. A beginning indicates the origination of a perfection in relation to what follows, and an endpoint in relation to what precedes. How could knowledge of that which has neither beginning nor end have either? Thus one who has a beginning, though no end, cannot encompass knowledge of It.
changes.reason: Restores the concluding ولا نهاية: the source says a knower with a beginning and no end, not one bounded at both ends; restores omitted reasoning and relative scope.

changes.old_en: **Al-Mahāʾimī:** In this intimate prayer the Prophet indicates both that he has attained the end of ends in knowledge and that he cannot encompass the full Reality. “I seek refuge in Your good pleasure from Your displeasure” considers the unity of divine acts as manifested in their effects. This follows the form of demonstration from a cause or agent to its effect. “I seek refuge in You from You” considers essential unity through direct witnessing.
changes.new_en: **Al-Mahāʾimī:** In one of his intimate invocations, the Prophet indicated what we have said: that he does not encompass the reality of knowledge, despite reaching its end of ends. He said, ‘I seek refuge in Your good pleasure from Your displeasure,’ in view of the unity of the acts, which are effects of these [attributes]. This follows the method of a demonstration of the reason why, inferring the effect from its agent. He then said, ‘I seek refuge in You from You,’ in view of the unity of the Essence, by the method of witnessing.
changes.reason: Corrects causal direction: acts are the effects of the named attributes, rather than acts being manifested in their own effects; retains the contrast of demonstration and witnessing.

changes.old_en: “I cannot enumerate praise of You” indicates effacement in the unrestricted Essence while acknowledging the impossibility of knowing it. “You are as You have praised Yourself” indicates subsistence through Him and His attributes: he knows by Him, not by encompassing His unrestricted Essence.
changes.new_en: He then says, ‘I cannot enumerate praise of You’—[understood as] effacement in the unrestricted Essence, while indicating his lack of knowledge of It. He then says, ‘You are as You have praised Yourself’; thus he subsists through Him and through His attributes, ... enraptured by Him, not through his own essence [the wording around عال، والها is uncertain].
changes.reason: Does not silently normalize the corrupt wording بالغناء / عال والها; restores the omitted enrapturement and avoids adding ‘encompassing His unrestricted Essence’ as the meaning of لا بذاته.

changes.old_en: The explanation “I cannot reach all that is in You” expresses precisely this combination. Even the Prophet's subsistence by God does not entail his subsistence in the Essence considered with absolute unrestrictedness; rather, it is through the Essence under a determination along with Its attributes. The prayer combines inability to encompass the absolute, which would be required even for the complete knowledge of what is below it, with actual attainment of the supreme end in knowing the Real. Subsistence (*baqāʾ*) is the furthest station, because at that point neither the Real veils creation nor creation veils the Real. In effacement (*fanāʾ*) creation is veiled; in concentration on generated beings the Real is veiled.
changes.new_en: Since the purpose of citing the prayer is to show the absence of encompassing knowledge together with attainment of the end of ends, Qūnawī explains ‘I cannot enumerate praise of You’ as ‘I cannot attain all that is in You’ in respect of unrestrictedness. Even if I subsist through You, my subsistence is not through Your unrestrictedness, but through Your determination together with its attributes. The Prophet thus combines an indication that encompassing the unrestricted Essence—even what lies below It—is impossible, since proper apprehension depends upon You [the transmitted connective wording is uncertain], with an indication that his knowledge of the Real has reached the end of ends, where he subsists through Him. Subsistence is the highest station: there neither the Real veils creation nor creation veils the Real. This differs from the station of effacement, which veils creation, and from ‘bringing-into-being’ (al-takwīn), which veils the Real [the received term requires verification].
changes.reason: Restores subsistence THROUGH determination and the received word التكوين; removes unsupported paraphrase ‘concentration on generated beings’; flags rather than repairs uncertain syntax.

changes.old_en: Other identifications include jurists and scholars, those whose works leave them waiting between Paradise and Fire for permission to enter, those whose good and evil deeds balance, and further groups named in the transmitted exegetical debates: persons whose protection or kinship has lapsed, persons whose fathers or mothers have won divine approval but not both, children of polytheists, hypocritical show-offs, and people who lived between prophetic missions. This passage's transcription is particularly defective amid its list. Al-Mahāʾimī favours perfected knowers because the Qurʾān says the men of the Heights know all the parties by their signs. That discernment presupposes surveying their extremities and the realities beyond them. It is a mark of the utmost knowledge attainable by human capacity.
changes.new_en: Other identifications include jurists and scholars; people whose deeds fall short, who are held between Paradise and the Fire until God permits them to enter Paradise; and people whose good and bad deeds are equal. The next identification is corrupt in the supplied text (بطارت خفائرهم إلى آخر الناس). Another corrupt phrase concerns fathers' approval without mothers' approval, or the reverse. Further suggestions are the children of polytheists, those who act for show, and people of the interval between prophetic missions who did not change their religion [the transition that follows is corrupt]. The chosen interpretation is supported by God's saying that its men recognize everyone by their marks. They are called ‘men’, understood here as the perfected, and their recognition of everyone by their marks is a distinctive property of surveying the extremities of every group. This can occur only at the utmost reach of knowledge: knowledge of the things whose extremities one surveys must reach the point that affords an outlook upon what lies beyond them, so that those things are properly known to the extent of one's capacity.
changes.reason: Replaces invented meanings for corrupt tafsīr identifications with explicit uncertainty; restores the relation of outlook, boundary and knowledge without falsely supplying intelligible prose.

changes.old_en: The wording “within the taste of perfection” implies that this expression directly names the intended matter. It has two relations: the intermediary between each pair of consecutive stations below the absolutely highest, and the relation of the higher of those stages to the still higher station.
changes.new_en: He says here ‘within the taste of the station of perfection’ to indicate that this expression signifies it directly. It has two relations: one between any two stations among those below the absolutely highest; the other concerns [the absolutely highest] and what lies only one degree below it.
changes.reason: Corrects the two relations: the second relates the highest station to the one immediately below, not an unspecified higher pair; brackets the connective supplied from the ensuing explanation.

changes.old_en: Under the first relation it is the *barzakh* joining two stations: the intermediate boundary that both separates and combines, like the line between shadow and sunlight. Those who have attained perfection are not halted at a fixed stopping-point, which is why this is not simply called *mawqif*. Under the second relation the highest encompassing boundary is the *barzakh of barzakhs*, higher than all the lesser intermediaries. Some also use *barzakh* for the presence of *wāḥidiyya* or the first determination as the origin of the intermediary realities, calling it the first, greatest or most comprehensive *barzakh*.
changes.new_en: Under the first relation it is the *barzakh* joining two stations: the intermediate boundary that both separates and combines, like the line between shadow and sunlight. Those who have attained perfection are not halted at a fixed stopping-point, which is why this is not simply called *mawqif*. Under the second relation the highest encompassing boundary is the *barzakh of barzakhs*, higher than all the lesser intermediaries. Some also use *barzakh* for the presence of *wāḥidiyya* and the first determination as the origin of the intermediary realities, calling it the first, greatest or most comprehensive *barzakh*.
changes.reason: Preserves the source conjunction between wāḥidiyya and first determination rather than presenting alternative descriptions.

changes.old_en: Qūnawī calls it the “unseen of the Identity” because the Identity itself may be apprehended through determinations. He calls his expression an *allusion* because no statement literally and adequately describes that unseen. Language presupposes apprehension, and ultimately convention, both of which presuppose a determinable object. “Unseen” is not a proper name that would restrict the Essence to the state of hiddenness; it merely signals that the Reality cannot be apprehended under this aspect.
changes.new_en: Qūnawī says ‘the unseen of the Real's Identity’ because the Identity itself can be apprehended within determinations. He says ‘allusion’ because no expression signifies it directly: expression presupposes apprehension—or, more precisely, a linguistic convention that itself depends on apprehension. ‘Unseen’ is not a name for it that would constrain it by hiddenness; the word is introduced only to indicate that it cannot be apprehended.
changes.reason: Corrects the order of dependence among expression, convention and apprehension; removes the added requirement of a determinable object.

changes.old_en: **Qūnawī:** “His true unity, which effaces all considerations, names, attributes, relations and associations, consists in the Real's intellection of Himself and apprehension of [this unity] in respect of His determination. Although this determining intellection and apprehension follows the unrestrictedness indicated, in relation to the Real's determination in every act of intellection ...”
changes.new_en: **Qūnawī:** ‘His true unity, which effaces all considerations, names, attributes, relations and associations, consists in the Real's intellection of Himself and His apprehension of Himself insofar as He is determined. Although this determinate intellection and apprehension immediately follows the unrestrictedness indicated, in relation to the Real's determination within the intellection of every ...’
changes.reason: Corrects the antecedent of لها from ‘this unity’ to نفسه (Himself), and prepares the page-bound continuation with متعقل as conceiver.

changes.old_en: ... of anything intellectually conceived, in every self-disclosure, it is an unrestricted determination, the widest of determinations; it is witnessed by the perfected, is the essential self-disclosure, and belongs to the highest station of unification.”
changes.new_en: ... conceiver, in every self-disclosure, it is an unrestricted determination and the most encompassing of determinations. It is the witnessing of the perfected; it is the essential self-disclosure, and to it belongs the highest station of unification.’
changes.reason: Restores متعقل as a conceiver, not a conceived object, and preserves witnessing wording and page-spanning quotation.

changes.old_en: **Al-Mahāʾimī:** True divine unity has no plurality whatsoever. It effaces even conceptual considerations, and a fortiori the names, attributes, relations and connections, since each implies multiplicity. This does not entail the abolition of attributes altogether but their inclusion within the unity without distinguishing them from the Essence so qualified. It is the Real's intellection of Himself before the distinctions among act of knowing, knower and known are made. These distinctions arise through His intellection of Himself and therefore are conceptually posterior to it. It is an intellection of the Essence insofar as It is intelligible, not yet a distinct personal specification; the latter would stand much farther from unrestrictedness. Attribute-distinction presupposes attribute-intellection, which in turn presupposes intellection of the Essence; here the Essence alone is apprehended.
changes.new_en: **Al-Mahāʾimī:** True divine unity has no plurality whatsoever. It effaces even conceptual considerations, and a fortiori the names, attributes, relations and connections, since each implies multiplicity. This does not entail the abolition of attributes altogether but their inclusion within the unity without distinguishing them from the Essence so qualified. It is the Real's intellection of Himself before the distinctions among act of knowing, knower and known are made. These distinctions arise through His intellection of Himself and therefore are conceptually posterior to it. It is the Real’s intellection of Himself in respect of determination as intelligible, not determination by individuation; the latter would stand much farther from unrestrictedness. Attribute-distinction presupposes attribute-intellection, which in turn presupposes intellection of the Essence; here the Essence alone is apprehended.
changes.reason: Renders التشخيص as individuation rather than personal specification; preserves the contrast of intelligibility and individuation.

changes.old_en: The intellection is true unity, for the act of intellect is not separated from knower and known. Unity considered along with distinct attributes, by contrast, includes a plurality of considerations. This unity is qualified as a “determination” only from the relevant perspective; at the level of unrestrictedness even unity has no privilege over multiplicity.
changes.new_en: This intellection is true unity: the intellection itself is not intellected alongside it, let alone a knower and something known. This differs from unity considered together with the attributes, which contains a plurality of considerations. This intellection is qualified as being ‘in respect of determination’, because in respect of unrestrictedness unity has no priority over multiplicity.
changes.reason: Restores the reflexive structure لم يتعقل معها التعقل and the a fortiori clause فضلا عن; they are more specific than absence of separation.

changes.old_en: Al-Mahāʾimī then expounds the first determination: relative to negative unrestrictedness it is determination, but relative to everything below it—including the Real's determination within every act of intellection or self-disclosure—it is unrestricted. Under this twofold aspect it gathers the determinations while remaining the most universal. Essential disclosure reaches the Muhammadan Reality immediately and others through mediation. He describes this disclosure as not appearing in differentiated loci: were it to shine on them as such, their differentiating constitution could not withstand it. It appears to the Essence in the Essence and is witnessed as such by one who has passed through effacement and subsists through God. This is essential unity, above the unity of attributes and intellect. Above it unity itself cannot be considered, for unity and plurality have no priority there.
changes.new_en: He then indicates that this is the first determination: ‘This intellection’—that is, self-intellection—‘and determinate apprehension, although it immediately follows the indicated unrestrictedness’, meaning unrestrictedness in the negative sense, would properly be qualified by unrestrictedness in ordinary usage and would thus not be a determination [in that respect]. Yet it combines both: determination in relation to what precedes it, and unrestrictedness in relation to what lies beneath it. Relative to the Real's determination in the intellection of every conceiver, whether the Real or creation, in every self-disclosure, in a locus of manifestation or otherwise, it is an unrestricted determination. In combining both it gathers the determinations [the connective wording here is uncertain], and it is that to which knowledge of Him relates. Hence it is the essential self-disclosure that falls upon the Muhammadan Reality directly, and upon others through an intermediary. It cannot disclose itself in loci of manifestation: if it shines upon them, it burns them up. It appears only to His Essence in His Essence; none sees Him thus except one who has been effaced in Him and subsists through Him. To it belongs the highest station of unification, essential unification above that of attributes and intellect. Unification cannot be considered in what lies above it, since the attribution of unity has no priority there at all. Understand.
changes.reason: Restores omitted ordinary/negative unrestrictedness distinction, the two relative aspects and full disclosure logic; replaces interpretive softening with the actual burn-up image and flags uncertain connective.

changes.old_en: **Text Eight. Qūnawī:** “A noble, universal text containing sublime mysteries.” The previous text established the Real as the end of any felicitous traveller. This text examines the source and differentiation of that felicity. Its mysteries concern the modes of self-disclosure in loci of manifestation, humanity as the complete locus capable of all such disclosures, and their consequences. Created happenings are not simply an other opposed to the Real, for their underlying realities and ...
changes.new_en: **Text Eight. Qūnawī:** ‘A noble, universal text containing clear mysteries.’ **Al-Mahāʾimī:** Having stated in the preceding text that the traveller who receives some felicity from the Real must have the Real as his final end, he now explains the cause of that felicity and its details. The mysteries discussed here are the kinds of self-disclosure in loci of manifestation, the human being as the complete locus calling for these kinds of disclosure, what follows from each self-disclosure, and that temporally originated things are not other than the Real, since He has not exerted an effect upon their realities or upon ...
changes.reason: Restores جلية as clear, and the actual causal claim لم يؤثر rather than adding ‘not simply an other opposed to’ or suppressing agency.

changes.old_en: ... their existence are not themselves altered; rather, the diversity concerns the relations of existence to realities and their forms. Therefore neither the many nor their temporal emergence negates divine unity or the necessity of unrestricted existence. This text will go on to describe apparent reciprocal influences and other profound matters whose worth is known fully only to God and those endowed with their knowledge.
changes.new_en: ... their existences, but upon the relations of existence to the realities or their forms. Thus their multiplicity and temporal origination do not impair unification or the necessity of unrestricted existence. He also explains the effect of each upon the other, and other matters that will appear at the end of the commentary on this text. These are the great mysteries whose worth is known only to God and His people.
changes.reason: Restores the scope of causal influence and the disjunction أو; removes unsupported ‘not themselves altered’, ‘diversity concerns’, and ‘apparent’ qualifications.

changes.old_en: Hence some theoreticians conclude that existence has become numerically multiplied through different essences or has acquired their limitations after being unrestricted. They overlook that the relevant change belongs to the *form in which something appears*, not to the underlying reality ...
changes.new_en: Hence most theoreticians say that existence has become multiple through the essences and has become conditioned by these loci of manifestation after its unrestrictedness. They do not recognize that this is an effect upon the form of what is reflected, not upon its reality ...
changes.reason: Corrects أكثر (‘most’) from ‘some’ and restores connected assertions rather than alternative explanations joined by ‘or’.

changes.old_en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continued):** Qūnawī speaks of a hidden secret in the degrees of reckoning because an apparently nominal relation may ultimately return to a more essential one. Al-Mahāʾimī argues that since names return to the Essence, even a severe reckoning under some names is not independent of mercy, though it may appear in a form of chastisement. A consequence can be fitting in a rational sense and manifest a perfection of wisdom while being painful to the recipient's natural disposition. He further conjectures that in the next world reason may come to predominate over bodily inclination; since the disclosures experienced by those undergoing punishment must be nominally determined, he proposes that punishment will in one respect come to an end. He attributes a corresponding doctrine to Ibn ʿArabī. This is a substantive theological claim of the commentator and should be indexed separately from Qūnawī's quoted formulation, not generalized without qualification to every Akbarian school.

He construes the phrase “if its outcome is a stronger relationship to the Presence of the Essence” as the necessary conclusion of a correctly formed argument, unlike relations under particular names, which can shift. Qūnawī uses restrictive language to assign freedom from reckoning to gifts with an effectively essential predominance, so as not to imply that every gift outside the first-mentioned class must be reckoned.

The reason given for absence of reckoning is essential proportionality between agent and recipient: an essential correspondence, unlike a contingent nominal condition, does not cease. Al-Mahāʾimī locates its governing character in mercy, arguing that the relation of mercy to the Essence is prior to that of wrath. A residual name-based aspect in a mixed gift may tempt one to expect reckoning, but a merely subordinate aspect does not override its governing essential correspondence.

**Qūnawī:** “Whoever does not know this foundation does not understand the reality of the saying, ‘God provides for whom He wills without reckoning’ (Q 2:212), nor the secret of ‘This is Our gift; bestow it or withhold it without reckoning’ (Q 38:39), and similar passages repeated in the Mighty Book and in prophetic reports, such as the saying that seventy thousand of his community will enter Paradise without reckoning ...”
changes.new_en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continued):** ... reckoning while others do not. He emphasizes this because he is certain of it, and speaks of a great secret that cannot be divulged. Its explanation is that the names return to the Essence. Thus reckoning, even when difficult under some names, returns to that in which there is no reckoning: mercy, even if it takes the form of punishment. Since punishment is His judgment, it bears a rational appropriateness to their acts, and it contains a perfection of wisdom in which one takes pleasure as regards intellect, although one suffers as regards nature.

Perhaps in the next world intellect will predominate in them over nature. Moreover, the disclosures to those undergoing punishment must be disclosures of the names; their punishment must therefore come to an end in some respect, namely the one we have described. Shaykh Muḥyī al-Dīn explicitly stated this. This relation has already been discussed because of its frequent occurrence in reality. If the outcome—that is, the effect of the prevailing and subordinated aspects—is a strong relation of those gifts to the Presence of the Essence, the expression used indicates that this outcome necessarily follows, just as the conclusion follows from a sound syllogism. This differs from relation to the names, which is not necessary, since it may change.

‘That, then, is what [has no reckoning]’ uses a restrictive construction to indicate that, of these two classes, absence of reckoning belongs exclusively to this one. Had this restrictive formula been used of the essential gifts [mentioned first], it would have suggested that reckoning is necessary for everything else, including this class.

He then gives the reason for absence of reckoning in both places: ‘Because essential gifts’—those mentioned first—and what has a stronger relation to them, this last class, issue from the agent and are received by the recipient only through an essential correspondence in both. What belongs essentially never ceases or comes to a halt. This pertains specifically to mercy, since mercy's relation to the Essence precedes wrath's relation. Because the aspect of the names is evident in the last class, one might suppose that it is without reckoning from the side of the Essence but subject to reckoning from the side of the names. He rejects this: nothing necessitates the gifts except that correspondence; the subordinated aspect has no effect. Understand.

**Qūnawī:** ‘Whoever does not know this foundation does not know the reality of God's saying, “God provides for whom He wills without reckoning” [Q 2:212], nor the secret of His saying, “This is Our gift; bestow it or withhold it without reckoning” [Q 38:39], and similar passages repeatedly mentioned in the Mighty Book, and also in prophetic reports, such as the saying that seventy thousand of his community will enter Paradise without reckoning ...’
changes.reason: Restores continuous translation rather than summary; removes translator directives from running prose; preserves the strength and qualifications of the commentator's punishment argument and the restrictive-construction reasoning.

changes.old_en:
**Qūnawī (concluding his report):** “... and with every thousand another seventy thousand.” These, he says, possess nominal gifts whose relationship to the Presence of the Essence is stronger than their relationship to the Presence of particular names and attributes; for that reason they follow those who possess essential correspondence and share in their states. Know this.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The foundation teaches that gifts essentially related to the divine Reality, and those in which that relation prevails, are without reckoning. Without it one cannot understand the explanatory ground of Q 2:212, “God provides whom He wills without reckoning.” Though the verse mentions divine willing and the comprehensive name “God,” which embrace named determinations, the essential aspect may predominate within the relevant bestowal. The comprehensive name includes Essence and attributes without lowering the Essence to the level of a particular name. Likewise divine will, here understood as distinct from restricted volition, has a more encompassing relation.

The expression “without reckoning” is taken to embrace the occurrence and timing of provision. The deeper mystery of Q 38:39, “This is Our gift: bestow it or retain it without reckoning,” refers to an essential gift not governed by a calculable rule of obligation or recompense—even the teaching or guidance through which realized people return from the Real to creatures can be transmitted or withheld without a corresponding numerical account.

Qūnawī uses the word “reality” for the first scriptural passage because its basis is accessible through names outwardly known, but “secret” for the second because it concerns the Essence, the deepest unseen mystery. The prophetic narration is then used to exemplify two groups entering Paradise without reckoning: the original seventy thousand, who are described as leaders with essential gifts, and the accompanying multitudes, whose gifts involve names but incline strongly toward the essential Presence. This is an interpretation of the report, not a hadith-critical authentication.

[The modern footnotes on this page cite al-Tirmidhī, Ibn Mājah and Aḥmad; they are excluded from the author's Arabic text and may serve as leads for an independent hadith check.]
changes.new_en:
**Qūnawī (continued):** ‘... and with every thousand, seventy thousand.’ These possess gifts of the names, but their relation to the Presence of the Essence is stronger than their relation to the Presence of the names and attributes. For this reason they follow those who possess essential correspondence and share in their states. Know this.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Whoever does not know that essential gifts, and those whose relation to the Essence predominates, have no reckoning does not know the reality of ‘God provides for whom He wills without reckoning’ [Q 2:212]—that is, the cause explaining it by a demonstration of the reason why. This is a gift of the names in which the relation to the Essence predominates, as shown by the fact that ‘God’ is a name encompassing the Essence and attributes, while the Essence is exalted within it. He is high in His nearness and near in His height. Likewise, mashīʾa is above irāda, so it too has a relation to the Essence. ‘Without reckoning’ means in occurrence and timing.

Nor does such a person know the secret of ‘This is Our gift’ [Q 38:39]: an essential gift that entails neither obligation nor recompense, even from the aspect of guidance for which the perfected are returned from the Real to creation. Bestow it by teaching whomever you wish, or withhold it, for it is ‘without reckoning’; that is why this phrase is placed last.

He first says ‘reality’, indicating something established in hearts because it concerns the manifest names; he then says ‘secret’, indicating that it concerns the Essence, which is the greatest of the unseen mysteries. He adds that the prophetic reports likewise state that these two classes of gifts are without reckoning: those related to the Essence alone, and those whose relation to the Essence predominates. The first class is the seventy thousand; the report indicates this by making them those who are followed.

The second class is those indicated by ‘with every thousand, seventy thousand’. These possess gifts of the names, but their relation to the Presence of the Essence is stronger because the aspect of necessity predominates.
changes.reason: Restores omitted statements about nearness/height, mashīʾa above irāda, the placement of ‘without reckoning’, and predominance of necessity; removes invented qualifications and modern hadith notes from running translation.

changes.old_en: **Qūnawī:** “Having described the classes of gifts and their governing rules, let us describe the kinds of recipients. Those who receive fall into differing ranks according to the requests that their preparedness, actual state, rank, spiritual constitution, natural temperament, or adventitious natural conditions express—the latter finding expression through the speech of the requesting recipient.”
changes.new_en: **Qūnawī:** ‘Having described the classes of gifts and their governing rules, let us describe the classes of their recipients. In receiving them they fall into levels, differentiated according to their requests of preparedness, state, rank, spirituality, natural temperament, or adventitious nature, which are expressed by the tongue of the seeking recipient.’ **Al-Mahāʾimī:** Having finished with the classes of gifts—essential gifts, gifts of the names, and those related to both—and what follows from them, he describes the classes of their recipients. Their reception differs in degree, so the gifts are also divided according to their classes. He explains that their levels multiply according to their requests.
changes.reason: Restores the commentary actually present in this Arabic pair, previously displaced into the next English pair; preserves the list without collapsing preparedness into spoken petition.

changes.old_en: **Al-Mahāʾimī:** Having divided gifts into essential, nominal and jointly related types, Qūnawī now divides recipients according to the different ways in which reception is possible. The word “request” (*suʾāl*) here is broader than a spoken petition. The first form includes a readiness or receptive condition arising through the Most Holy Effusion (*fayḍ aqdas*) at the level of divine affairs; a second concerns requests connected with the fixed entities; a third pertains to a rank of manifestation generally, under the ordered stages of descent. A fourth comprises requests specific to particular levels, such as the spiritual—spirit, heart and soul—natural temperaments resulting from bodily elemental constitution, and contingent bodily impulses and acquired conditions.
changes.new_en: **Al-Mahāʾimī:** The first class is requests of state; the receptive state [the wording here is uncertain] is preparedness, the receptivity bestowed by the Most Holy Effusion upon the divine affair. The second is requests described as ‘purified from the fixed entities’ [المقدسة عن الأعيان الثابتة: the construction is uncertain]. The third is requests of rank, encompassing every rank among the ranks of descent. The fourth is requests specific to certain ranks: spiritual requests, related to the spirit and what corresponds to it, such as heart and soul; requests of natural temperament, related to the body insofar as it is composed of the elements; and requests of adventitious nature, which arise according to impulses originating in the bodily faculties.
changes.reason: Restores the source's numbered classes and identifies rather than silently smoothing the unstable first and second clauses; removes explanation carried over from previous pair.

changes.old_en: Only some requests, especially those springing from natural appetites, receive verbal expression once formed in the heart. **Qūnawī:** “In summary, the highest rank of recipients in receiving the Real's influx and gifts is to perceive the face of the Real within the conditions and causes called intermediaries and throughout the ordered series. Such a recipient knows whence he takes, and witnesses that the causal intermediaries are nothing other than determinations of the Real at divine and cosmic levels, diverse as their kinds may be. That is to say, between the received divine effusion and the recipient there is nothing but the effusion itself becoming determined through restricted receptivity, without any additional ruling of contingency being attached to it through its passage across the successive intermediary ranks or becoming coloured by their contingent judgements.”

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Every category of recipients admits further degrees. At their highest, those who receive through preparedness, a spiritual state or some other request behold the divine aspect in both the one original effusion and the particular gifts in which it becomes articulated. They thus recognize the face of the Real both in causes and in conditions.

A *condition* (*sharṭ*) is something upon which an occurrence depends but which does not by that fact produce it; a *cause* (*sabab*) is something on which it depends with a causally effective relation. The distinction is not erased by saying that both function as mediating links (*wasāʾiṭ*) between the first effusion and its recipient. The ordered series concerns beings that emerge through their respective levels, from the divine ranks onward to the human ...

**Qūnawī:** ‘In summary, the highest rank of recipients in receiving what comes to them from the Real's effusion and gifts is to see the face of the Real in the conditions and causes called intermediaries, and in the chain of ordered sequence. The recipient thus knows and witnesses that the causal intermediaries are nothing other than determinations of the Real in the divine and cosmic ranks, with all their different kinds. This means that between the received effusion of the Real and the recipient there is only the effusion's own determination through qualified receptivity, without the addition of a contingent ruling required and necessitated by the effect of the effusion's passage through the intermediary ranks and its being coloured by the rulings of their contingencies.’

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** In every class of recipients distinguished by the requests already mentioned there is a further gradation. The highest rank of recipients—whether they receive through a request of preparedness, state or otherwise—is qualified by ‘in their receiving’ [the following explanation of this qualification is unclear in the supplied text]. He uses the singular for the Real's effusion because it is originally one, and also mentions His gifts, which articulate that effusion. He mentions both to indicate that their vision of His face follows one and the same course in undifferentiated and differentiated reception: they see the face of the Real in conditions and causes.

A condition is that upon which something depends without its exercising an effect on it; a cause is that upon which it depends together with an effect. Mentioning both indicates seeing His face in what exercises an effect and what does not. They are called ‘intermediaries’ because they intervene between the first effusion and the recipient, and ‘the chain of ordered sequence’, that is, the order of the beings proceeding by effusion from divinity to ...

changes.old_en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The ordered chain extends as far as the human level. Qūnawī names both conditions and causes to show that mediating terms are not confined to conditions. A proximate cause is itself a mediator between the ultimately effective principle and the recipient, and a remote cause still more obviously so. The series of causal influence differs from the broader series of ordered beings: conditions are not necessarily constituents of the former though they are included in the latter.

The highest recipient sees the face of the Real in all these links. The one who possesses theoretical knowledge understands how reception occurs; one who possesses direct witnessing sees it immediately. In this account the mediators are not separate self-subsistent agents over against the Real, but His determinations at the levels of names and attributes, and at cosmic levels such as fire in burning or water in drowning. The manifest disparity and apparent lowliness of some worldly causes do not imply that such forms fall outside the doctrine of determination, nor that all determinations must have equal rank or perfection. Their differences belong to relational and perspectival orderings (*nisab wa-iʿtibārāt*), not to a newly acquired plurality in the unrestricted Essence.

Two propositions are required to clarify this. The first is that nothing independently other than the first intelligible (*maʿnawī*) effusion intervenes between that effusion and a sensory recipient; rather, the effusion itself becomes determined by the receptivity appropriate to an ordered divine or cosmic rank. The qualification “intelligible” is deliberate: an observer confined to sensory causation may suppose the successive mediators to be alien realities added between the first effusion and the tangible recipient. But the claim is not about a merely sensory stream of physical effects.

No separate contingency-property is superadded to the effusion merely as a result of passage through the intermediary ranks or through its being described as “coloured” by their possibility. Qūnawī mentions both that something *requires* and that it *necessitates* a result, so that voluntary and necessary accounts of operation are both covered. Al-Mahāʾimī insists that a governing determination actually belongs to its appropriate locus; the contingent rulings of intermediary things reside in those intermediaries and cannot be transferred wholesale as if the same accident inhered in two distinct subjects. His final premise uses the scholastic maxim that one and the same accident does not inhere in two subjects.
changes.new_en:
... humanity.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** He mentions these two designations to indicate that both encompass causes and conditions. Intermediaries are not restricted to conditions: a proximate cause mediates between the true agent and the recipient, all the more a remote cause. Nor is the chain of ordered sequence restricted to causes: although conditions do not enter the chain of agents, they enter the chain of ordered beings. Thus one sees the face of the Real in all of them. The recipient knows this if he belongs to the people of knowledge, and witnesses it if he belongs to the people of direct vision.

He mentions causal intermediaries particularly because, if these effective things are identical with the Real despite their apparent independence and do not subsist through their own essence, non-effective things have still less claim to independence [the intervening wording is unstable]. They are nothing other than determinations of the Real in the divine ranks, such as names and attributes, and the cosmic ranks, such as fire and water in burning and drowning, despite the different kinds of causes and conditions. This indicates that the lowliness of some does not prevent them from being His determinations because of His exaltedness; nor should one say that, if all were His determinations, they would be equal or close in degree. Their disparity arises only from relations and considerations.

Their being identical with the determinations of the Real depends upon two premises. First, between the Real's first, non-sensible effusion and the recipient among sensible things there is nothing except that first effusion's own determination through receptivity qualified by a divine or cosmic rank. The qualification ‘non-sensible’ is needed because the veiled person imagines many intermediaries other than the effusion between it and a sensible recipient, but imagines no intermediary between a sensible effusion and its recipient. Without the qualification one might suppose that the sensible effusion was meant, and the argument that the intermediaries are identical with the non-sensible effusion would not be established.

No contingent ruling is added to that non-sensible effusion, such that the combination of effusion and ruling would mediate between the effusion and the recipient. The contingent ruling in question is what the effect of the effusion's passage through the intermediary ranks ‘requires’ and ‘necessitates’. He uses both terms to include operation by choice and by necessity. He mentions the ‘effect’ so that one does not suppose that passage alone imposes a contingent ruling on the effusion without affecting it. That is not so: a thing's ruling is its established effect. This effect is the effusion's being coloured by the rulings of the intermediaries' contingencies. The evidence that such rulings are not added to the effusion that passes through the intermediaries is that those rulings subsist in the intermediaries, and a single accident does not subsist through two causes [the supplied word بسببين requires verification].
changes.reason: Replaces interpretive summary with continuous translation; restores the two chains, causal-intermediary reasoning and exact subjects; does not silently substitute ‘subjects’ for the received ‘causes’ in the final premise.

changes.old_en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The preceding argument grants that the effusion becomes determinate in passing through successive ranks, so that the mediators can be called determinations of the effusion. To conclude that they are determinations of the Real requires a second premise. Qūnawī states it as follows.

**Qūnawī:** “One sees that the effusion is a self-disclosure from among the disclosures of the Real's inward aspect. The multiplicity of determinations that occurs in it belongs to the rulings of the name the Outward (*al-Ẓāhir*), since the outward aspect of the Real is the site in which His inward aspect becomes disclosed. The rulings of outward appearance make multiple the absolute unity of inwardness. These rulings are what are called the recipients (*qawābil*), and they are nothing other than the forms of the divine affairs (*ṣuwar al-shuʾūn*). Understand: God speaks the truth and guides whom He wills to a straight path.”

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Effusion is specified as disclosure of the inward Real, not merely a disclosure under a particular outward aspect. The differentiated determinations of effusion depend on the multiplicity of its receptive loci; plurality as such is a ruling of the name *al-Ẓāhir*, under which what is inward becomes displayed. The unity of inwardness is not a unity opposed to the possibility of plurality; it comprehends that plurality without yet presenting it as distinct. Outward manifestation makes that intelligible plurality apparent in its several forms.

The rulings called “recipients” are identified with the fixed entities and with forms of the divine affairs. Since the form of a thing marks its determination, these are characterized as determinations of the Real, not a freestanding ontological population existing over against Him. In that restricted sense the intermediate terms are none other than His determinations. One must nevertheless preserve the sequence of explanatory steps: determining effusion is not synonymous with creating an extrinsic accident in the divine Essence; nor is a phenomenal difference asserted to be sheer nothingness.

Al-Mahāʾimī admits that this is what can be inferred from the expression under the perspective of unveiling. The full unity to which it alludes cannot be adequately stated in subject–predicate language: any verbal assertion contains at least a source and an asserted act, an agent and an object, or a subject and predicate. He identifies the “straight path” here with a tasted realization of unity that ordinary expressions cannot convey. The special reference to divine willing suggests, he conjectures, a bestowal of guidance outside acquisitive reasoning; proofs drawn from intellect or transmitted reports are not sufficient *as such* for this particular apprehension. This does not deny their validity in their own registers.
changes.new_en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Certainly, the effusion acquires a determination through passing through them; the intermediaries are therefore determinations of the effusion. That is one premise. The other is that the determinations of the effusion are determinations of the Real. This is explained by the Shaykh's words:

**Qūnawī:** ‘One sees that the effusion is a self-disclosure among the self-disclosures of the inward aspect of the Real. The multiple determinations that attach to it are the rulings of the name the Outward, insofar as the outward aspect of the Real is a locus of disclosure for His inward aspect. The rulings of manifestation multiply the unrestricted unity of inwardness. These rulings are what are called recipients, and they are the forms of the divine affairs, nothing else. Understand. God speaks the truth and guides whom He wills to a straight path.’

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This explains that the effusion's determinations are determinations of the Real: one sees the effusion as a self-disclosure among the self-disclosures of the inward aspect of the Real. He specifies this because the Real has many self-disclosures from the side of the Outward. Its being affected by multiplicity shows that it is a disclosure of the Inward: the effusion multiplies with the multiplicity of recipients, while multiplicities belong to the rulings of the name the Outward. Thus the effusion is the name the Outward, and the effusion is a self-disclosure of the Real through the Real, insofar as the outward aspect of the Real is a locus of disclosure for His inward aspect. The rulings of manifestation multiply the unrestricted unity of inwardness—that is, the unity belonging to the Inward [the connective wording is unstable]. This is unrestricted unity, not unity opposed to multiplicity; rather, it includes multiplicity.

The rulings of the name the Outward make that multiplicity manifest from it. Those rulings are called recipients, namely the fixed entities. The fixed entities are the forms of the Real's affairs. Thus the rulings in the name the Outward are forms of the Real's affairs, which are rulings of the name the Inward. The forms of a thing are its determinations; these are therefore determinations of the Real. Accordingly, the intermediaries are identical with His determinations, and a fortiori are nothing other than them. Understand.

This is what can be drawn from the expression that indicates unification by way of unveiling. God speaks the truth, which is unification itself, containing no multiplicity whatsoever. Otherwise, an expression necessarily indicates ‘unification’ as a verbal noun, ‘the one who unifies’ as an active participle, ‘what is unified’ as a passive participle, and a subject and predicate. He guides whom He wills among His servants to a straight path of tasted unification, which cannot be expressed. He qualifies this by mashīʾa because it is above irāda. Perhaps it is pure guidance—that is, acquisition has no part in it, since intellectual and transmitted proofs have no part there. He calls it the straight path because whatever lies below it is not free of a claim to partnership with God. Exalted is He above what they associate with Him.
changes.reason: Restores the full chain from Inward/Outward to recipients/fixed entities, literal effusion-as-Outward assertion, grammatical argument and final guidance claim; removes translator's unsolicited doctrinal qualifications and softening.
